summary: Lists requirements and use cases for optional administrative operations in the Internet Printing Protocol, covering printer and job administration and a new Device object that models a single output device. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Printers need a boss mode for pausing a printer or managing jobs. This lists what that boss mode should be able to do.

subtitle: Administrative operations needed to manage printers and print jobs over the Internet

tldr.problem: The Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) version 1.0 focused on end-user printing, but operators and administrators need additional operations to control printers, manage jobs, and maintain output devices in production environments.
tldr.mechanism: This requirements document specifies 21 administrative operations organized into two parallel groups: Printer operations (which manage the print service software) and Device operations (which control the physical output hardware).
tldr.outcome: Implementers can develop consistent administrative interfaces for printer management, with separate operations for pausing, disabling, resetting, and powering devices, enabling graceful maintenance and emergency control.

facts.value: 13 distinct operations for managing print services

facts.label: Design principle
facts.value: Separate operations for clarity rather than operation attributes that change behavior

facts.label: Conformance
facts.value: No required dependencies between Printer and Device operation sets

today: RFC 3239 remains an informational requirements document for IPP administrative operations. It has not been obsoleted and continues to guide the design of printer administration interfaces in IPP implementations and related printing systems.

sections.title: Printer Administration Needs
sections.content:
The Internet Printing Protocol (IPP) in version 1.0 and 1.1 supports end-user printing operations but lacks the administrative operations necessary for production environments. This requirements document defines what optional administrative operations should exist for managing printers and print jobs.

The document separates administrative operations into two distinct categories: Printer operations that affect the IPP software abstraction (the print service), and Device operations that control the physical output device hardware. This separation makes implementation options clear and allows systems to support one category, the other, or both.

A key design principle is that each distinct administrative capability should have its own operation rather than using operation attributes to alter behavior, making capabilities discoverable through the standard operations-supported attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: The original print protocol was just about sending documents to printers. But real-world printers need admin powers, so this document says what those powers should be.

sections.title: Printer Management Operations
sections.content:
Printer operations manage the IPP software service and how it handles print jobs. Essential operations include enabling and disabling the printer (preventing new job acceptance while letting current jobs finish), pausing after the current job completes, and resuming processing.

For administrative maintenance, the Deactivate-Printer operation makes the printer read-only by combining disable, pause-after-current-job, and rejection of other operations except queries and configuration. The Activate-Printer operation restores normal function.

For emergency recovery, Restart-Printer recovers from software confusion by reinitializing the IPP printer software while saving volatile state if possible. Shutdown-Printer gracefully powers down the printer service without a protocol-level way to bring it back (though Startup-Printer can bring up a new instance on an already-running host).

The Hold-New-Jobs and Release-Held-New-Jobs operations allow operators to pause accepting new jobs while letting them accumulate in a held state, useful when reconfiguring output devices.
sections.plainLanguage: You can tell a printer to stop, pause at the next safe point, lock it for maintenance, reset it if it's confused, or shut it down completely.

sections.title: Device Control Operations
sections.content:
Device operations control the physical output device hardware. Disable-Device prevents the device from accepting any new jobs from any protocol, while Enable-Device restores operation. These differ from Printer operations because a single output device may be controlled by multiple print services.

Emergency pause operations include Pause-Device-Now (immediate pause regardless of consequences, for emergencies) and Pause-Device-After-Current-Copy (pausing at a convenient point like after the current copy or job). Resume-Device restarts operation after either pause.

Pause-Device-After-Current-Job pauses at a device-defined boundary without breaking up multi-copy jobs, useful when emptying output bins. Deactivate-Device makes the device read-only for maintenance (like replacing toner), while Activate-Device restores function.

For power management, Power-Off-Device shuts down the hardware after saving state, and Power-On-Device powers it back up. Reset-Device recovers from hardware or software confusion (similar to a device MIB reset).
sections.plainLanguage: You can pause a device right now in an emergency, pause it at the next safe point, lock it for repairs, reset it, or turn it completely off.

sections.title: Use Cases and Implementation
sections.content:
A typical use case for Pause-Printer-After-Current-Job is when an operator wants to gracefully stop the print service at the next job boundary without losing current work. This operation is also implicitly invoked by Deactivate-Printer and Shutdown-Printer.

Device operations enable field service scenarios: a technician can Deactivate-Device to make the output device read-only while replacing staples or toner cartridges, ensuring no new jobs start while maintenance proceeds. Another scenario uses Pause-Device-After-Current-Copy when the output bin is nearly full, allowing the operator to empty it between copies.

The operations are designed so Printer and Device implementations have no conformance dependencies: either set of operations may be supported independently. When a document is produced defining these operations, they will be registered according to IPP procedures for new operations.

Security is essential: these operations are for operators and system administrators only. Implementations must authenticate users and verify authorization before allowing administrative operations, preventing unprivileged users from disrupting print services.
sections.plainLanguage: An admin can pause printing between jobs for maintenance, a technician can lock a device to replace toner, and the system won't let regular users do admin stuff.
